paragraphs.text: II. EXCERPTS FROM REMIGIUS'S COMMENTARY ON THE PASCHAL SONG

In the Catalogue of Illustrious Men, that is, in the book that blessed Jerome began and his disciple Paterius completed, we read who this Sedulius was. He was at first a layman devoted to worldly wisdom. Afterwards, having turned to God, he wrote this book as a kind of "dirocheum" [?], that is, a double refreshment, drawn from the Old and New Testaments. It should be noted that he first wrote it in prose and later put it into verse. He gave it the title Paschal Song and dedicated it to the priest Macedonius. For it was the custom among the ancients to present their writings to wise and noble men, so that the writings would be strengthened by their authority and protected from rivals. He taught partly in Asia and partly in Italy. Now he writes a letter to Macedonius. "Decurso" ("having run through"): finished; it is a participle with no verb to derive from. "Censeas": you would judge. "Severitatis" ("of severity"): of gravity. "Obiurges": you would reprove. "Suffultus" ("propped up"): helped; "fulcio" means "I help", and so a "fultor" (supporter) is named from helping. "Paschalis" ("paschal"): evangelical. "Maiestatis" ("of the majesty"): that is, of Christ, as the apostle says: Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. "Pelagus" ("sea"): the depth of the sea is called "pelagus", but here it stands for the depth of the divinity. "Tyro" ("recruit"): a new and untrained soldier who has just entered the service of Christ. "Lintre": a small boat. He uses figurative language here. Above he called the depth of the paschal mystery an "immense sea"; now he says "a small skiff" for "a small talent". "Expurgem": I will excuse. Here he excuses himself to Macedonius for having dared to compose this book in prose, and afterwards in verse. "Audacem": presumptuous. "Devotum": humble. He calls the breast a harbour because many ships gather in a harbour, and in the same way many thoughts are carried on in the breast. "Naufragium" ("shipwreck"): to have fallen into no heresy. "Occupatus" ("occupied"): held back... "Non utilitati" ("not to usefulness"): not to spiritual teaching. "Sed inani" ("but to empty"): to worldly wisdom. "Deprehenderem": I would assign. "Lusibus" ("to games"): he calls worldly poems "games". "Fabricam" ("his workmanship"): me, made by him. "Condivit": seasoned, salted, filled. "Oculos cordis" ("the eyes of the heart"): he means the mind's sight. The eye ("oculus") is named as if "ocior lux", "swifter light", because it quickly looks at whatever it attends to, or else because it is shown to be hidden ("occultus") by the eyelids that cover it. "Sentes": "sentes" are thorns; likewise they are called, in a shortened form, "spinae", and the word is declined in the plural. Hence "dumosi agri", thorny fields. By the thorns of the thorny field he means worldly learning. "Nisu": with effort. "Cultum": service. "Procella" ("storm"): anxiety. A wave is called "procella" from "percellere", "to strike", because it strikes people's minds. "Aegros anhelitus" ("sick gasps"): sighs, just like yours. "Quamvis ipsi": he honours Macedonius by saying "ipsi" for "ipse". "Igniculum in me" ("a little spark in me"): you think, he says, that I have some little spark of wisdom. "Silicis" ("of flint"): flint is a very hard stone from which fire comes out. "Ne non carerem": so that I might not lack. "Creditam" ("entrusted"): given to me by God. He calls his talent the amount of one talent. Here he touches on the gospel parable that says: A certain man, going on a journey, called his servants, e. d. d. t. a. d. a. n. [?]. The five talents are understood as the five bodily senses; the two as understanding and action; the one as understanding alone, because there are some to whom understanding is given without the grace of acting. These are the ones who, so to speak, dig it into the ground when they do not share it with others. This is what he means by "lue non carerem" ("that I might not escape the penalty"), namely the guilt of those who bury their talent. "Proclivioris lubrici" ("of the steeper slipperiness"): of inclination. "Unum" [?] is taken as fixed, as if he said "of a steeper slipperiness"; it is not in use. "Lubrum" is the name for smoothly planed wood that is not level, and so a slippery ("lubrica") thing is one that is not level, on which we slip; but here it stands for sin. "Clipeus" is the name for a larger shield. In Greek "clepte" means "to steal", and so "clipeus" comes from "kleptein ta somata", from stealing bodies. "Mellitum": sweetened. He calls the catholic faith the way of liberty, because true liberty is found there. "Qua occasione" ("on whatever occasion"): whether in verse or in prose. Prose is unbound speech. "Egregius" ("outstanding") is named as if "e grege", chosen out of the flock: someone set apart from the flock for his merit and holiness. In the same way "eximius" comes from "eximere", to separate. "Remissioribus alis" ("with more relaxed wings"): with lowered wings. When the eagle flies high it holds its wings spread out, but when it goes down to the ground it draws its wings in. In the same way, you ought not always to read lofty scriptures. He says this on account of his own poem. We use "antistare" to mean "to excel", and so a bishop is called "antistes" because he goes before all, excelling them. "Tyrocinio": that is, in the first period. We call "tyrocinium" the first period of military service. Recruits ("tirones") are raw soldiers, boys, who trained at the post in the Field of Mars, striking blows sometimes with the edge and sometimes with the point. The man who instructed them was called the "campidoctor". "Pacatus": peaceable, because at the time when Sedulius wrote this book the Alans and Vandals were ravaging Italy. "Astutiam" ("shrewdness"): wisdom. "Astutia" comes from "astu", an indeclinable noun. "Gallicanum aeque": likewise a priest, like the others. "Mitissimum": very gentle. "Mitis" is said as if "mutus", "silent". "Eruditus" ("learned"): "rudis" means new, and so "eruditus" means one taken, as it were, out of the countryside ("rus"), led away from ignorance and set in the bosom of learning. "Simplicitatem columbae" ("the simplicity of the dove"): Laurentius has the simplicity of the dove, because, like the dove, he takes care neither to deceive another nor to be deceived by another. "Vere felicem" ("truly happy"): the poet plays on the name.

"Idoneos" ("suitable"): formed. "Idos" in Greek is "forma" in Latin. Jerome used to send his writings to noble and distinguished people of the Church, men and women, such as Chromatius and Heliodorus, Paula and Eustochium. "Domicilium": properly a "domicilium" is an upper room, because it is in the upper part of the house, like the eyebrow ("cilium") on the higher part of the body. "Syncletices": a personal name. "Ministrae" ("servants"): deaconesses. "Syncletos" in Greek means consul or senator, and so "Syncletia" means a senator's lady. "Allecta": joined. He plays on the name when he says "senate": because in this present life she was called "sena" [?], may she deserve to enjoy the angelic senate in the life to come. "Castum" ("chaste"): restrained. We call "castum" what is tightly bound, and on the other hand "incestum" what is loose. "Refertum": filled. "Posset et docere" ("she could even teach"): teach as well. Yet the apostle forbids women to teach in church, saying: Let women be silent in church. "Nomine meritoque" ("by name and by merit"): he plays on the name, for she was Perpetua by name and perpetual by merit. "Teneram" ("tender"): young. "Nuptae" ("of a bride"): of a betrothed woman, because a married woman ought to wear ornate clothing. Up to this point he speaks in the person of Macedonius; from here on, in his own person. "Deterreas": you would make afraid; for "deterrere" is to drive someone away by threats. "Implesti" is a shortened form of "implevisti", "you have fulfilled". "Omnia omnibus factus es" ("you have become all things to all"): as the apostle says: To the Jews I became like a Jew, to the Gentiles like a Gentile. I have become all things to all, so that I might save all. He did not say this to lure them in, but because he wanted all to be saved. "Iactura": loss. Properly, "iactura" is the jettisoning sailors do at sea: when a storm arises, the cargo is thrown into the sea to lighten the ship. "Ne pigeat" ("let it not irk you"): let it not make you sluggish. "Anchoram" ("anchor"): firmness. He keeps up the metaphor, because above he spoke of the depth of the gulf of the paschal song, and now he says "anchor" for strength. "CKVPA" [?] in Greek means hand, and so an anchor is an iron hand, which bites into the ground and holds the ship motionless. "Our Passover." The Passover of the Jews was the one sacrificed toward evening. Our Passover is Christ, who was sacrificed for our sins, as he says: "our Passover", meaning of Christians, not of Jews, "Christ has been sacrificed". They had a Passover of cattle, but we have a divine one. When he says "with the Father and the Holy Spirit", he shows that they are equal in divinity, because the Arians said "grace to the Father in the Son", claiming that the Son is less than the Father.

‘Paschales’: solemn, festal. He addresses the reader metaphorically in the guise of a dinner guest, inviting him to the paschal poem as though to a supper. By ‘paschal feasts’ he means the heavenly mysteries. ‘Dignatus’: a participle used in place of the verb ‘dignare’ (to deign). He says ‘accubitare’ (to recline at table) because the ancients ate lying down. ‘Supercilium’ (brow): the ‘cilium’ is the part of the body, the skin, by which the eyes are covered; the Greeks say ‘cillere’ for ‘to move’, and so ‘cilia’ are named from moving, just as ‘palpebrae’ (eyelids) are named from ‘palpitare’ (to flutter). Hence the hairs that stand out above the eyes are called ‘supercilia’. Here ‘supercilium’ is used for pride, which is detected chiefly in the eyes. ‘Pone’ stands for ‘depone’ (lay aside), and it is an aphaeresis. He calls this poem ‘paschal’ because it narrates the deeds of that Lamb of whom it is said, ‘Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.’ ‘Cognoscas’: you may understand. Between ‘cognoscere’ and ‘agnoscere’ there is this difference: we ‘come to know’ (cognoscimus) those we have never seen, and we ‘recognize’ (agnoscimus) those we have already seen. ‘Amicum’ (friend): ‘amicus’ is as if ‘animi custos’, guardian of the mind, or ‘animi aequus’, equal in mind. ‘Artificis’: artful. An artful book is one composed with pomp and keeping to worldly eloquence, whereas the divine books consist of bare and simple words. ‘Saciare’: to fill, as if he were saying, ‘You ought to be filled with spiritual food rather than bodily food.’ ‘Cibus’ (food) is cooked nourishment, fit for human eating only, for the other animals live on raw food. Hence among the Greeks both man and food are called ‘brosis’, because man alone among the animals uses cooked food. ‘Cenis’: poems. The sense is: if you are regarded as fastidious, that is, haughty, so that you think our poem worth nothing because it is modest, then feed your mind on the poems of the secular poets. ‘Caenon’ in Greek is ‘common’ in Latin; hence ‘caena’ (supper) is named from sharing, because among the ancients many ate there together. In the same way ‘convivium’ (banquet) is named from living together, which the Greeks call ‘symposion’. But Cicero says that the Latin ‘convivium’ is the better word, since it comes from living together, whereas the Greeks call it ‘symposium’ from drinking together. ‘Quicquid volat’ (whatever flies): all kinds of birds. He speaks allegorically. There are three branches of philosophy, and he touches on them here: Ethics, Physics and Logic. By the sea is understood Ethics, the moral [?] part, which discusses human conduct; by the land, Physics, which treats of the nature of all things; by the stars, Logic, the rational part, which speaks of divine matters. ‘Carpsimus’: we have taken. He keeps up the metaphor: by the garden he means a small talent, by the vegetable a modest poem, by the earthenware dish the perishable body, fragile and made of clay. Hence the Apostle says, ‘We have a treasure hidden in earthen vessels,’ that is, in our bodies. ‘Grandisonis’: in grand-sounding poems. There are three styles: the low, the middle and the grand, and Virgil touches on all of them. ‘Tragico’: cheap. For ‘tragos’ in Greek is ‘goat’ in Latin; hence the Greek ‘tragemata’, cheap little gifts, called ‘colobidia’ [?] in Hebrew and ‘bellaria’ (sweetmeats) in Latin. Geta is a comic character in Terence. The Getae themselves are a Moesian people, jesters far too fond of games. ‘Contagia’: vices, crimes. ‘Contagium’ is the name of a disease of swine, so called because through the contact of one animal it spreads to many; the same is ‘porrigo’ (scurf), from ‘porrigere’ (to extend), because it extends from one to others. ‘Monimenta’: remembrances. A ‘monimentum’ is a memorial, because it reminds (moneat) the mind. ‘Niliacis biblis’ (with Nile papyrus): the Nile is a river of Egypt, and the ‘biblus’ grows there. The ‘biblus’ is a large rush, also called papyrus, from which the ancients made books; for ‘bibli’ in Greek is ‘libri’ (books) in Latin. And the Nile is so called as if ‘Neonilus’, bringing down new mud. ‘Odas’: praises. ‘Resonare’: to sound together, as we read in the psalm: ‘On a ten-stringed psaltery I will sing to you.’ But this is not taken to refer to the psaltery but to the ten commandments of the Law: he calls the Old Testament, in which the ten commandments of the Law are contained, ‘ten-stringed’. The psaltery is a musical instrument with ten strings; it is struck from below and resounds from below. By ‘odes’ he means the psaltery of ten strings, and by ‘ten strings’ the ten commandments of the Law. ‘Arcibus’: in dwellings. A citadel (arx) is the higher building in a city, named from ‘arcere’, to repel, because it repels the enemy far from itself, which is also called an etymology [?]. ‘Sceptrum’: rule. It is something a king carries, and it is used to mean kingship. God is called the Beginning either because he is without beginning or because all things that exist took the beginning of their being from him. ‘Medullis’: in minds. The marrow (medulla) is the inner part of the bones, so called because it is in the middle (media). ‘Curis’ (cares): ‘cura’ is so called because it burns the heart (cor urat). ‘Serpit’: it penetrates. ‘Cecropei’: Cecrops was a king of the Greeks steeped in poisonous doctrines; hence his evil teaching is called the Cecropian poison. ‘Spirantis odorem’: this is a hypallage, for he ought to have said, ‘following the fragrance of the life that breathes’. ‘Pedorem’: stench. ‘Pedor’ properly means the stench of feet. ‘Pagi’ (villages): ‘page’ in Greek means a spring; hence a village is so called, because it is situated beside a spring. Hence country folk are called pagans, because they are far from the city of God, or because they drink, as it were, from a single spring. The Labyrinth was an underground pit, which Daedalus made. The story goes like this. Pasiphae was the wife of Minos, king of Crete. She fell in love with a bull and, on the advice of Daedalus, who was the most skilful of craftsmen, she lay with it. From this the Minotaur was born, half man and half bull, who ate human beings. Seeing this, Daedalus made an underground pit with a hundred doors, in which the Minotaur was shut up. He called this dwelling the Labyrinth, and it is called ‘Laborintus’ as if ‘labor intus’ (toil within), because whoever once went in never came back. Hence the poet metaphorically calls the errors of the Athenians a Labyrinth, since they delight in worthless poems more than in the true words of the Gospel reading. In reality, Taurus was a secretary of King Minos who lay with Pasiphae, and hence the name Minotaur. Daedalus was a most skilful craftsman, and skilful people are called by his name. Hence we call those who speak deceitfully ‘logodaedali’. ‘Labruscam’: the ‘labrusca’ is the name for the wild vine, so called because it grows on the edges (labra) of roads. ‘Uva’ (grape) is so called as if ‘uvida’ (moist); that is, with the pleasant grapes of the Gospel reading. The ‘saliunca’ is a foul-smelling flower like a rose, named from ‘salire’ (to leap) because it grows quickly; in Greek it is called ‘orcitunica’ [?]. He puts the saliunca for paganism. ‘Fana’ (shrines): ‘fone’ in Greek means voice; hence a temple is called a ‘fanum’ because oracles were given there, and ‘profanus’ means, as it were, ‘far from the shrine’, that is, far from the temple of God. ‘Metallis’: images. A ‘iuger’ is as much as a yoke of oxen can plough in a day. ‘Plagas’: regions. There are five zones of the world, three uninhabitable and two habitable. By ‘poisons’ he means the secular poems about worthless things, which lead a person down to hell. ‘Vireta’: green places. ‘Amoenum’ (pleasant) is so called as if ‘amunium’, a place without duty (munus), suited only for pleasure. ‘Per latices’ (through the waters): through baptism. ‘Animantur’: they are given life. This is what we read in the Gospel: ‘Whoever is thirsty, let him come to me and drink, and out of his belly will flow rivers of living water.’ He said this about the Spirit, which those who believed in him were to receive. ‘Ut messis’ (like a harvest): the gathering of God. By the granaries he means the heavenly mansions. ‘Merx, mercis’ means profit; ‘merces, mercedis’ means reward. ‘Omnipotens’: the poet's prayer. ‘Omnipotens’ is compounded from the noun ‘omnia’ (all things) and ‘potens’ (powerful), a participle that properly belongs to God. It is one of the words that have no comparison, which is made by increasing or diminishing. For the Almighty is he whose power can be neither increased nor diminished, and so cannot be compared. The simple word ‘potens’ is so called as if ‘patens’ (open), because all things lie open to him. ‘Aeterne’: ‘aeternum’ is derived from the Greek ‘eon’, which is taken to mean perpetual. ‘Deus’ (God) is interpreted in Greek as ‘fear’, but it comes from the Greek ‘theoro’, I see. Here Sedulius has kept the custom of the ancient poets, and especially of Virgil: he has stated his theme, invoked, and narrated. ‘Procella’ (storm) is so called because it strikes (percellat) people with fear, or ships with the waves. The sun (sol) is so called because it alone (solus) appears by day. The moon (luna) is so called as if ‘lucina’, and she is also Juno. Among the pagans she is called Lucina because, in the pagans' ravings, she presides over those being born into the light (lux). The moon is horned as it waxes and wanes. ‘Qui stellas’ (who [numbers] the stars): Hyginus and Aratus were astronomers who pretended to know the number of the stars, but they lied, for no one knows it except God. ‘Potestates’ (powers): because there are some that rule over heat, others over cold, others over storms. ‘Diversa in corpora’ (into various bodies): ‘corpus’ (body) is named from corruption, because it can quickly be dissolved. Here he wants ‘body’ to be understood as everything that is perceived by the five senses, or whatever is brought forth by the right hand. The Greeks say ‘mysticum’ for ‘secret’; hence secret things are called mystical, and there are the words ‘mysterium’ (mystery) and ‘symmistes’, a confidant. ‘Arca’ (the ark): the ark is so called because the things it contains are secret (arcana), hidden from us. Now he gives the allegory of what the ark signifies. ‘Diluvium’ (the flood): just as those who were in the ark were saved while the others perished, he says, so now, through baptism, in which faith in the Holy Trinity is contained, the faithful are saved and the unbelievers condemned. For the flood signifies sin, and the water of the flood signifies baptism. ‘Callis, callis’ (track): ‘callis’ is named from the ‘callus’, the beaten path of cattle, along which the cattle go. ‘Semita’ (footpath) is so called as if ‘semis via’, half a road. ‘Via’ (road) is named from ‘vehere’ (to carry), as if ‘vehea’, or, as Augustine says, ‘via’ comes from the force (vis) of feet, because it is worn down by feet. There are four kinds of roads: the track, the footpath, the road, and the ‘actus’. The ‘actus’ is a public road that takes two carts or two wagons, one going and the other returning. ‘Hiemps’ (winter): ‘hiemps’ is named from the hemisphere, which is half of the heavenly sphere. ‘Vernare’ means to flower; hence the springtime (vernale tempus), because then the whole world flowers. ‘Patentem’: open. By the ‘open forest’ he means the multitude of miracles. ‘Sidera’ (stars) are named from ‘considerare’ (to consider), or as if from the verb ‘sidero’, ‘mico’ [?], which means ‘I move’, because they move together with the heavens. ‘Pectus’: the lungs, for the voice comes out of the lungs. ‘Bibulus’: ‘bibulus’ means one who drinks a great deal. After his invocation he gives his narrative. ‘Chaos’: chaos means the primordial confusion. ‘Vivacibus’: long-lived. ‘Vivax’ means one who lives long; hence Virgil's ‘the horns of the long-lived stag’. ‘Abusque’ and ‘adusque’ are used for ‘ab’ and ‘ad’ (from and to). ‘Naturae’: because it belongs to human nature that a person should die, even after a hundred years. Death is the loss of life; according to Augustine, ‘mors’ (death) is named from the bite (morsus) of the forbidden fruit. ‘Grandaevo situ’: in extreme old age. ‘Situs’ is used for old age. Properly, ‘situs’ means the mould of the earth in neglected places that the sun cannot reach. Here ‘situs’ is used for great age. He says ‘frigidus’ (cold) because in the young the blood is warm, but in the old it is cold; so ‘frigidus’ means old. ‘Cum seniore viro’ (with an older husband): because Abraham was already old, since Abraham was a hundred years old and Sarah ninety. According to Varro, old men (senes) are so called as if ‘se nescientes’, not knowing themselves, because in extreme old age they lose their wits. ‘Plus pietatis habens’ (having more devotion), that is, toward God. In this Abraham was cruel, in that he was willing to behead his son, but devout, because he loved God more than his son. ‘Occumberet’: should die. Now he gives the allegory: Abraham signifies God the Father, Isaac the Son, and the ram the humanity. We believe in two natures in Christ and one person; and just as the ram was sacrificed while Isaac remained unharmed, so the humanity of Christ submitted to the passion, but the divinity was incapable of suffering. ‘Lot’ is interpreted as ‘turning aside’, and ‘Sodom’ as ‘dumb beast’, because they sinned irrationally against nature. ‘Chaos’: the confusion of the elements; it signifies the destruction of the world. The story is well known. God rained fire and sulphur on Sodom, after an angel had commanded Lot and his wife to flee and not to turn their faces back. His wife looked back and was turned into a pillar of salt; and fittingly into a pillar of salt, so that by this example the minds of the hearers might be seasoned, lest by doing similar things they suffer similar things. ‘In sua terga’ (behind him): if a ploughman does this, he will make a crooked, winding furrow or wound the legs of the yoked oxen. By the ploughman he means the preacher, and by the ploughing the preaching, the very speech itself. For just as the ploughman must not turn his face behind him, so the preacher must not do the things that he preaches should be avoided. ‘Frondea’ is used for ‘frondosa’. ‘Frondosum’ means having leaves, while ‘frondeum’ means something made of leafy branches, such as a bower, a shade. ‘Plexos’: coiled. ‘Trisulcis’: three-forked. A snake moves its tongue so quickly that it seems to people to be three-forked. The ‘chelydrus’ is a snake that lives on land and in water. ‘Cherson’ in Greek means land and ‘ydor’ water; hence ‘chelydrus’, as if ‘chersydrus’, because it can live on land and in water. ‘Incedens’: entering. ‘Baptisma’: ‘baptisma’ is Hebrew; it is ‘balneum’ in Greek and ‘lavacrum’ (washing) in Latin. ‘Rude’: new. ‘Hic et haec rudis et hoc rude’ is of all three genders and means ‘new’; but when it means a rod stripped of its bark, ‘rudis’ is feminine. ‘Rudus, ruderis’ is neuter and means crushed tile or the rubble of walls. Moses was a type of Christ, as we read in the Apostle: ‘All were baptized in Moses, in Christ.’ For just as the people of Israel were saved in the Red Sea under Moses and the army of the Egyptians was destroyed, so we too are saved in baptism under Christ, and the devil with his adversaries is defeated. ‘The voice of the Lord cries out over the waters.’ There are four elements. Two of them are joined together in lightness, fire and air, for they always move upward; two are joined together in heaviness, earth and water, for they always fall from above to the depths. ‘Abyssum’: by the abyss he means the vast depth of the scriptures, for an abyss means a vast depth. ‘Nimbis’: with rains. A ‘nimbus’ is a heavy and sudden rain, and it is called ‘nimbus’ as if ‘nubus’, from the clouds (nubes), just as ‘imber’ (shower) is as if ‘umber’, from the shade (umbra). ‘Nectaris’: of sweetness. Nectar is a general name for all sweet things. ‘Siccus’ (dry) is so called as if ‘sine suco’, without juice. By ‘metal’ he means anything hard. Christ was the bread, because he gave them bread, as he himself said, ‘I am the bread of life.’ Christ was the rock, because he gave them water, as the Apostle says, ‘And the rock was Christ.’ Christ was in the waves, because he led them through the sea. ‘Rudenti’: braying. ‘Ruditus’ is properly the voice of asses, as bleating is that of sheep. ‘The sun stood still at Gibeon’, over against Gibeon; it is a metropolitan city. ‘Arma’ (arms) are so called because they cover the shoulders (armi). ‘Famulata’: obedient. Jesus son of Nun and Joshua are the same, and the name is interpreted as ‘saviour’. ‘Sine more’: contrary to custom, because ravens usually snatch food rather than serve it. ‘Avido’: greedy, gluttonous. ‘Ales’ (bird) is named from its wings (alae); the raven (corvus) from the hoarseness of its voice. ‘Heredem’ (heir): Elisha. ‘Heres’ (heir) is named from ‘haerere’ (to cleave), or from ‘erus’, master. ‘Astra’: the stars are named from ‘astreus’, an astronomer. ‘Sulcos’: furrows. Three elements make a furrow: the air is divided by an arrow and water by a ship, but they quickly close up again, while in earth the furrow remains; fire takes no furrow, but turns whatever it finds into itself. ‘Helias’ (Elijah): if the a is changed to o and the accent falls on the last syllable, it becomes ‘helios’, the sun. ‘Helias’ is interpreted ‘God, mind, Lord’: ‘hel’ God, ‘i’ mind, ‘as’ Lord. ‘Cetus’ (sea monster) is masculine in Latin but neuter in Greek, τὸ κῆτος, plural τὰ κήτη; hence we read ‘cete grandia’ (great sea monsters). In Hebrew it is called Leviathan. ‘Depositum’: what was entrusted. ‘Spirante’: helping. Babylon, which Nebuchadnezzar had raised up. ‘Achemeniam’: Achemenes, king of the Parthians, was of such fury that once he grew angry he could in no way be appeased until twelve men had been sacrificed. This king had his wrath. ‘Nil urente rogo’: the fire burning nothing. A ‘rogus’ (pyre) is a heap of logs. ‘Vecors’ (senseless) means without a heart (cor); ‘ve’ is used for ‘not’, as in ‘vesanus’, not sane. We say ‘pecudes’ of smaller animals and ‘pecora’ of larger [?] ones. ‘Septena tempora’: seven years. This is the whole for a part, for each year has four seasons. ‘Hirsutus’: hairy, because his hair and nails had grown like those of eagles. ‘Nec minus’, that is, ‘likewise’: this is the figure called litotes, when two negatives make one affirmative. ‘Tyranni’: among the Greeks ‘tyrannus’ is used for a king, but among the Latins for one who seizes another's property. ‘Belua’ (beast) is a trisyllable, a resolution in the metre, and he has put the singular number for the plural, for there were seven lions. ‘In faucibus’: ‘fauces’ are the jaws, and they are called ‘fauces’ from ‘fage’, that is, to eat. ‘Dic ubi’ (tell me where): by way of recapitulation he addresses Nature with a question, and the poet makes her answer him in a certain way. ‘Qui tartara’ (who [harrowed] hell): now he introduces her as if answering him. ‘Anum’: an old woman. Sarah suffered two things, for she was old and barren. ‘In anguem’: into a serpent. ‘Nimbis’: with rains. God rained manna on the children of Israel; when they saw it they said ‘man hu’, which is interpreted ‘What is this?’, and so that food is called manna. ‘Volucres’ (birds) are named from their frequent flight (volatus). ‘Tria lustra’: three periods of five years. To the man Hezekiah [?]. The Greeks reckoned their times by Olympiads, that is, by four-year periods, but the Romans by the lustrum, that is, by five-year periods, because in the fifth year the sun renews its rising. For the first year has 365 days and a quarter, and so do the second and third years, but the fourth has 366 days, because four quarters make one day; this is the leap day, which is inserted every fourth year. In the fifth year the sun begins the same courses again. For example, in the first year the sun is at the forehead of the Ram, in the second at its shoulders, in the third at its side, in the fourth at its loins, but in the fifth it returns again to the forehead. ‘Lustrum’ is also named from ‘lustrare’ (to purify), because every fifth year the Romans used to purify the whole city with candles and lamps in honour of their gods, just as we do every year in the month of February in honour of Saint Mary. But ‘lustra’ in the plural means the lairs of wild beasts. ‘Naufragus’: one who suffers loss at sea is called a ‘naufragus’ (shipwrecked man). ‘Naus’ in Greek is ‘navis’ (ship) in Latin; hence ‘naufragium’ means the breaking of a ship. ‘Caminus’ and ‘clibanus’ are Greek, and ‘fornax’ (furnace) is Latin. ‘Rictus’ is a wide opening of the mouth; it comes from the verb ‘ringo’, I open my mouth. ‘Instimulante’: provoking. A ‘stimulus’ (goad) is properly a rod with iron at the tip, with which oxen are urged on. ‘Nempe’: it is no wonder, he says, if these things were done against nature. ‘Quocumque’: in whatever direction. ‘Vana’, or ‘fana’: idols. ‘Sinistro’: perverse. The poet grieves over the errors of the pagans. ‘Idolum’ (idol) is a diminutive from ‘idea’, form. ‘Dementia’: ravings. For a ‘lira’ is the furrow of a plough; hence ‘deliro’ means I go off the track, I stray from the way of reason. Properly, ‘delirare’ is when oxen stray out of the furrow; so too old men are said to ‘delirare’, because they depart from correct speech. ‘Bovem’: Apis, for Apis was the name of the bull that was offered to Queen Isis. ‘Semihominemque’ (and the half-man): the ape, for the ape is half man and half dog. There are three kinds of apes: one is shaggy and is called the sphinx; another, which has a tail, is called the cercopithecus; the third, without a tail, is called the ape (simia), and it has a face and feet like a man's, but the rest of its body like a dog's. ‘Ut volucrem ibin’ (like the bird the ibis): he means the domestic Egyptian storks, which the Egyptians worshipped because of the snakes they devoured. ‘Geminum’: equal. He has put ‘twin’ for ‘equal’, because those three days at the beginning of the world were equal; but after the sun was created on the fourth day the days are unequal, for they either lengthen or shorten, except only at the equinoxes. ‘Fugantur’: they are darkened. This is poetic, because the stars (stellae) are named from ‘stellare’, to shine. ‘Lignee’ (wooden one): a man who worships wood is called wooden, just as one who worships stone is called stony. ‘Surdis’: to the deaf. ‘Surdus’ (deaf) is so called because it keeps in the filth (sordes) of the head; ‘mutus’ (dumb) is named from ‘mugitus’ (lowing), because it keeps the sound of the voice in the nostrils. ‘Culmina’ (roofs) are named from ‘culmus’ (straw). ‘Carduus’: the thistle is a thorny plant, commonly called ‘calcatripa’. ‘Monstra’: idols; ‘idea’ means form. ‘Dulia’ means servitude; hence idolatry is the service of idols, and a man who serves idols is called an idolater. ‘Montem’: by the mountain he means the arduous poem of the Gospel. ‘Tolis’: the ‘tolus’ is the top of the roof, from which the timberwork proceeds. ‘Ubi dantur digna petenti’ (where fitting things are given to the one who asks): he touches on what is said in the Gospel, ‘Ask and you will receive.’ ‘Reprobus’: rejected. ‘Angulus’ (the corner): the people of the Jews [?]. That stone is Christ, who was rejected by the Jews when they said, ‘We will not have this man reign over us,’ and in the psalm: ‘The stone which they rejected,’ and so on. Christ is called the cornerstone because he joins to himself the Gentile people and the Jewish people, just as a stone joins walls. ‘Simplet’: may make single. THE STORY OF ARIUS. Arius was a teacher of the city of Alexandria, the metropolis of Egypt, which Alexander the Great built. Peter was bishop there, and under him Arius was the master of the school. He secretly taught that the Son was less than the Father, and the Holy Spirit less than both. Then Peter was sent to prison by Licinius, the colleague of Constantine, because of the catholic faith that he preached. Christ appeared to him in the form of a most beautiful boy, clothed in a tunic so dazzlingly white that he could scarcely be looked at, but torn as if by dogs. Then Peter, weighed down by the chains with which he was bound and unable to rise, cried out, ‘Lord, who has treated you so and torn you?’ The Lord said to him, ‘Arius has rent me, for he has divided me from my Father; but see that you do not hold communion with him.’ Later, after Licinius had been killed by Constantine because he wanted to seize Constantine's empire, Constantine assembled a very great synod, namely of three hundred and eighteen bishops, not counting deacons and abbots, and Arius was ordered to come there so that his faith might be laid open. As he was approaching the synod, while the holy bishop Alexander persevered in prayer, Arius was seized by such terror that all his bowels failed him in pain. Then he ordered a privy to be made ready for him. When he came to it, all his bowels poured out, because by the just judgement of God, just as he was empty in mind, so he was left empty in belly. ‘Curva per avia’ (through crooked trackless places): through the falsehood of perverse doctrine. An ‘avium’ is a place without a road (via); ‘a’ is used for ‘without’. ‘Nepos’: a ‘nepos’ is a son's son, and ‘nepos’ is as if ‘natus post’, born after. When it means grandson or granddaughter, it has ‘hic nepos’ and ‘haec neptis’; but when it means a profligate, it is ‘hic et haec nepos’. ‘Avi’: ‘avus’ (grandfather) is so called as if ‘avitus’, ancient. ‘Totum commune’ (all held in common): in the Holy Trinity there is communion, or community, except for the relative names. Whatever can be predicated of the Father can be predicated of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, such as good, great, merciful, almighty and so on, except, as was said above, for the relative names. ‘Quo crescat’ (whereby he should grow): he is perfect everywhere, not created. Arius said that he was a creature, but he lied, for he was not created but begotten. ‘Nam quia qui summus’ (for since he who is highest): the most exalted. Understand the force of the words: the Son is not the same ‘who’ (hic) as the Father, but the Son is the same ‘what’ (hoc) as the Father, one substance. There is a difference between ‘hic’ and ‘hoc’: ‘hic’ refers to persons, ‘hoc’ to substance. ‘We are one.’ He did not say ‘unus’ (one person) but ‘unum’ (one thing), that is, one substance. Arius ought to know ‘one’ as one substance. For he rightly said that there are three persons, but wrongly that there are three substances, for he said that the Son was less than the Father and the Holy Spirit less than both. Sabellius, on the other hand, rightly said that there is one substance, but wrongly that there is one person, for he said, ‘When he wishes, he is the Father; when he wishes, he is the Son; when he wishes, he is the Holy Spirit.’ This Sabellius ought to know the threefold faith. ‘Ast hic Arrius’ (but this Arius): a ‘cachinnus’ is loose, rippling laughter. This can also be applied to the philosophers. For one philosopher talks a great deal, like Epicurus, who said many things about the creation of the world, for he said that the world consists of atoms. Another is excessively silent, like the Pythagoreans, who learned for five years and meditated in silence for five years. The Peripatetic walks; the Stoic stands; Socrates loves weeping, for he wept continually because he saw the people of this world pursuing vices. Democritus ripples with laughter; he is said to have laughed continually because he saw people pursuing the avarice and shameful gains of this world. Hence Juvenal: ‘Democritus used to shake his lungs with perpetual laughter.’ ‘Vexilla’ (banners) are named from ‘vehere’ (to carry). A ‘vexillum’ is a military standard. ‘Ianua vos’ (you, the door): he makes an apostrophe to those who serve as soldiers of Christ. Christ is called the door because through him one comes to him. The door (ianua) is the beginning of the house, and it is named from the god Janus, to whom the beginning of every thing was consecrated. Hence the month of January is so called, because it is the beginning of the year. ‘In albo’: in the heavenly book. The ‘album’ was the tablet on which were written the names of those accepted into military service, and if any of them was killed, the letter theta, which signifies death, was written at the head of his name. ‘Tremit’: it resounds and says, ‘Prepare the way of the Lord.’ The lion has a great voice and is the king of beasts. Mark is depicted in the likeness of a lion because he began his Gospel with the cry, ‘the voice of one crying in the wilderness’, and because he describes the royal dignity of Christ. ‘Iuvenci’: of a bullock. The ‘iuvencus’ (bullock) is named from ‘iuvamen’ (help), because it gives people help in ploughing the land. The bullock was customarily sacrificed in the Temple, and Luke describes the things the Lord did in the Temple and around the Temple. John is represented by the eagle because, just as the eagle gazes at the sun with unflinching eyes, so John, soaring above all the heavens, [beholds] the divinity of Christ, which the other evangelists described [?]. ‘Proceres’: leading men. ‘Proceres’ properly means the corbels, the ends of beams that project in buildings. Hence leading men are called ‘proceres’ because they stand out among the rest. The month (mensis) is named from ‘mene’, the moon, because the months change according to the course of the moon. ‘Maniplos’ is the primary form, and ‘manipulus’ the diminutive from it; properly it means five hundred soldiers, the same as a cohort. By ‘sheaves’ (manipuli) he means good works. ‘Meto’ means I gather; hence the harvest (messis) is so called, because it is gathered every year. ‘Metior, metiris’ means I measure; ‘metor, metaris’ means I choose. From this point the poet begins to carry out what he promised, for he promised to write from Adam to the birth of Christ.

Primogenitum protoplastum: "the firstborn, first-formed man." Protos in Greek means "first" and plastus "formed"; so protoplastus means "first formed." De sede: "from his seat," that is, from paradise. Paradise means "garden of delights"; Adam means "earthly man" or "red earth." Illecebris: "by enticements," that is, by pleasures. Illecebrae are so called from illicere, to entice, to deceive. Heu, "alas": the poet grieves over the woman's fault. Noxia: "guilty." He puts a question to the woman: "O wife, were you more guilty, or that faithless serpent?" Then he answers himself: that faithless serpent, the deceiver; but you too are not free of blame, because you consented. In this passage there is a complete syllogism, made up of a proposition, an assumption and a conclusion. Perfidus, "faithless," is so called as if it meant "betraying faith"; for the devil lost faith when he said, "You will be like gods." He did not fulfil what he promised, for not only did they not become gods, they even became mortal. Demon is so called as if from daimon, "very [?]". Eve means "mother." Nongentos: "nine hundred." Adam lived nine hundred and thirty years, Methuselah eight hundred and eighty. Nepos primi terrigenae: "descendant of the first earth-born," that is, Adam's posterity. Fauces, "jaws," are named from the Greek phage, "to eat." Difficilis: "slow," because he does not always punish. Veniale: "deserving of pardon." God created two rational natures, the angel and man. The one sinned with no one persuading him and without being clothed in the frailty of a body, and so he perished beyond recovery; but man, because he was frail in body and sinned at the devil's persuasion, therefore earned pardon. Tensos: "swollen," heavy and laden. De limine: "from the threshold," from the beginning, from the entrance. Caro factum: "made flesh." This is synecdoche, the part for the whole, for a human being consists of flesh and soul. Clausa: "closed," that is, leaving the virgin intact. Prae natis: "above those born," above the sons. He took this from the psalm, where we read: "Beautiful in form above the sons, on whose fair lips grace is poured," because even in his humanity he was more beautiful than the rest. Obsitus: "surrounded." Salve: the poet greets the mother of Christ. Tenet: "rules." Giro: "in a circle"; just as a circle or crown seems to have neither beginning nor end, so does the dominion of Christ. Femina: femina and mulier, "woman," are not words denoting corruption, but sex and nature, for a virgin can be called both femina and mulier. Pastoribus: "to the shepherds." The shepherds were in the wilderness beyond Bethlehem near the Tower of the Flock, which is called Ader. If they felt any fear, they would climb it. There was a plain there, suitable and useful for flocks. Eous: as an adjective it is eous, eoa, eoum; eous as a noun is a part of the sky. Tyrannus: tyrannus is Greek; in Latin it is rex, "king." Among us a tyrant is one who seizes another's possession, which is why he calls Herod a tyrant. For he was a foreigner, with an Idumean father and an Arabian mother; he was brought up by Hyrcanus, high priest of the Jews, and when Hyrcanus died he seized the kingdom. Nubila: "clouds," that is, gloom of mind. Alens: "nourishing"; he was cheerful in face but gloomy in mind. Tractat: "ponders." Neglegis: "you do not understand," for he had read in the law of the Jews that Christ was to be born of Judah. Numina: "power" or "will," for will is taken for the accomplishment of the work. Patrandum: "to be accomplished." Alacres: "joyful," hastening. Thesauris: by "treasures" he means the cases or boxes in which the gifts were. Solutis: "fitted" [?]. By the gold they believed him to be the future king, by the frankincense God, by the myrrh mortal, because the bodies of the dead are embalmed with myrrh. The three magi signify the human race, spread by the three sons of Noah through the three parts of the world, Asia, Africa and Europe, because it came to Christ with three natural disciplines: physics, ethics and logic. Why three and not more? Because of the number of the Holy Trinity, or because of the three times, which God always beholds. Non repetamus iniquum: once we have come to Christ, let us not return to the wicked one, let us not go back to the devil, just as the magi did not go back to Herod. Herod means "of skin" or "glory of skin," and he signifies the devil, who, when the first parents had been stripped of their robe, clothed them in the garments of skin that belong to mortality. For once we have come to Christ through baptism, we must not go back to the devil, whom we renounced in baptism. Aperit: "reveals," that is, the anger he had been hiding, as he said above: "having clouds in his mind." Facinus: "crime"; what he wanted to do, he could not accomplish, for Christ had fled to Egypt. Facinus is a neutral term (to meson), for it is used of both good and evil. Inmerito: "unjustly." Vixdum, like agedum: dum is a syllabic addition. Vagitus: the first cries of infants; hence the god who presides over infants is called Vagiticanus. Innumerum nefas: "manifold sin." Orbata: "bereft" of her son. Lanio: "cruel one." This is a rebuke to Herod. The wolf is called lanio from lana, "wool," because it kills sheep, for laniare means to kill. Alieno in corpore: "in another's body," that is, in the bodies of the saints, as he himself says to Paul: "Saul, why do you persecute me?" He did not say "my saints"; from this it is clear that God suffers in the holy martyrs. Emeritus: "complete." We pronounce merere with a short e. Those soldiers were called emeriti who, on completing their fiftieth year, retired from military service and were given some rank; hence emeritus means wholly complete. Nec mora: "without delay." When Christ was twelve years old, he was found in the temple teaching. If anyone should ask why he said "without delay," when there is a long interval, as far as human reckoning goes, between twelve and thirty years, he answers by means of a phrase inserted in parenthesis with a question. Fluens: "being born." The poet is playing on words: it is no wonder, he says, that he prophesies without speech, since he has a mute father. Spiramina: we call the coils of ropes on ships spirae, and so some say that the revolutions of the eight months are called spiramina. But since there is no precedent for this, it is better to take taciturna spiramina, "silent breathings," as the outward and inward breaths of the prophet over the nine [?] months, without voice, until the birth of John. Tollere: in saying this he explains what he means by "coming to take away the sin of the world." Mihi: "for me," that is, for all, for he put himself in the place of all. Decutit: "drives out." Non obfuscata: "not darkened," not obscured. For just as light, when it enters darkness, takes on no obscurity but rather drives out the darkness itself, so Christ, though he took on flesh, nevertheless took into himself no stain of the flesh of sin. Attactu: "by his touch," that is, by his baptism. Flesh is sometimes taken to mean sin, and Christ is said to have borne sin when he took on the likeness of sinful flesh. Torrentum: "rushing"; it is both an adjective and a noun. Limphas: the Greeks say nymphas, we say limphas; for among the Greeks the sign for the same number, fifty, is N, which with us is L. Refluas: "flowing back"; this is a poetic usage. It happened when the children of Israel crossed the Jordan on their way to the promised land. Then the priests crossed first, and as soon as the water covered their feet, the part of the Jordan downstream fled and fell into the Dead Sea, while the part upstream stood in a single heap. The poet has applied this to the Lord's baptism. Harenas: "sands." When written without the h, arenae are named from their dryness (ariditas); but when written with the h, they are so called because they stick (haereant) to buildings. Honore: "he will be honored." Illa columba... [?] Mansuetum: "merciful." Mansuetus, "gentle," is so called as if "accustomed to the hand," kind. Mitem: mitis, "meek," is so called as if mutus, "mute," one who is thought to lack speech because of his great humility. God dwells in the gentle, as he himself says: "On whom shall my spirit rest, if not on the one who is humble and quiet and trembles at my words?" Per volucrem: birds (volucres) are so named from their frequent flight (volatus). The Spirit appeared as a dove to show that Christ is simple, and that he fills the hearts of those who love [?] through simplicity and innocence. The Father is shown in the voice, the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, the Son in the person of the man who was being baptized. The Father is there, the Son is there, the Holy Spirit is there: here he shows the Trinity. De caute: "from the rock," from hard stone. Cautes and cotes are the same thing. Vipereis: "serpentine," venomous. The viper is so called because it gives birth by force (vi pariat); for it has no womb, but is said to conceive through its mouth. Potestas: that is, angelic and archangelic power. It is no wonder that the devil, who is a spirit, could show Christ all the kingdoms of the world, since blessed Benedict, while still in the body, was able to behold the whole world, not because the world was made smaller, but because his mind was enlarged by the grace of contemplation. The devil tempted the Lord after his baptism to show that we are tempted more fiercely when he sees us abandon him and devote ourselves more diligently to the service of God. Delapsus: "let down," or descending. Labere: "throw yourself down"; it is the imperative of the verb labor. Fastigia: "the heights"; pinnacles are the tops, the highest parts of a house. Here, however, he has used it for the stories of the temple. The temple of the Lord was built in three stages, with three stories: from the ground to the first were thirty cubits, from the first to the second another thirty, from the second to the third sixty; that makes one hundred and twenty. Curvavit: "formed"; he says "curved" because the heavens are shaped like a vault. Vectus: "carried," by his own power, just as we read of the Holy Spirit in the passive, "the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters." For by what would he be borne, if not by his own power? Cuspide: "with the spear," by casting. He has called the word of God a sword; hence the Apostle speaks of "the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God," with which God strikes someone when he makes a sinner righteous. Praecipites: "falling." Confringens sapientia: "shattering the wise"; he has used sapientia as a neuter. God shatters the strong when he casts them down from the swelling [?] of pride and leads them to true humility. He destroys the wise when he overturns their vain wisdom and leads them to the true wisdom, which is Christ. God did not choose orators and philosophers and emperors, but the poor and the humble and fishermen. Tractare: "to pursue." Germanum: "brother," because we are brothers. Germanus properly means one springing as it were from the one seed (germen) of a father. Vetusti doli: "of the ancient deceit." The ancient deceit is original sin. It is called deceit because it was brought in by the devil's fraud; therefore we must wipe out from our hearts envy, which is truly the devil's mark. Degener, "degenerate," is the term for one who does not live up to the nobility of his parents, who shows himself ignoble by his deeds; we degenerate from God when we hate one another. Sicut benedicier idem: a great deal is to be understood here. Just as he commands that he be blessed by us, the very one by whom we are all blessed, so he commands that he be hallowed by us, the one by whom we are all hallowed. Iam iamque: an adverb of one wishing for something soon. The Lord reigns always and everywhere; we ask that he may gather us to himself and reign in us. Non succedunt: "do not come." Per aevum: aevum is used for perpetuity, and it comes from the Greek aion, "time." Time is nothing other than the course and alternation of things, as night follows day and day follows night. The crown stands for the eternal reward, because just as a crown has no beginning or end, so that reward will lack beginning and end. Nusquam means "in no place"; usquam, by contrast, "in some place"; just as numquam means "at no time" and umquam "at some time." Utque polo: by "heaven" understand the soul, by "earth" the human body. Ydrus: the hydrus is a water serpent. Vendicet: "may seize," and make his own. Artus: "limbs"; artus is so called from artare, to bind tight, because they hold the body together. Panem nostrum: "our bread." This is understood not as this bread but as spiritual bread, which is the Son of God, who is called substantial because he surpasses all substance or essence. And although dialecticians say that the category of usia applies to God, God is nevertheless beyond usia, and therefore, as far as human understanding goes, he is nothing, because he surpasses all understanding, as the Apostle says: "the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding." Annonam: "allowance," a salary; it is the same as a prebend. Annona is so called because it is renewed each [year]. Diurno: from dies, "day," comes diurnus, "of one day"; from diu, "long," comes diuturnus, "of a long time." Corpore illo: "by that body," that is, by the spiritual mystery. Verbumque cibusque: "both Word and food." Word, because he is God before the ages, begotten of God the Father; food, because although he was God he became man, so that he who was the food of angels might be the food of men. Cautio: "confirmation." Cavo, cavis, "I secure," has the perfect cavi; hence cautio means a confirmation. So in the Gospel, "take your bond" means your confirmation or written document. Tortoribus: "to the torturers," that is, to the demons. The ten thousand talents mean the greater sins, such as fornication, adultery and murder; the hundred denarii the lesser, such as anger, hatred and the like. If, then, we forgive our brothers the lesser sins, God will forgive us the greater; if not, we shall be bound more heavily, even though already released from our sins. Here he touches on the Gospel, where we read: "A certain man settled accounts with his servants." Donec: "until." He has put a finite term for an infinite one, because those who are to be damned in hell will never obtain pardon. It is not as Origen says, that after a thousand years Satan will be released with his followers; rather, the Lord's sentence will stand secure, in which he says: "The wicked will go into eternal punishment." So he has put "until" for "always," as we read in the psalm: "So our eyes are on the Lord our God until he has mercy on us," that is, always. Brevem: "very small." Amen: this particle is the sign and as it were the seal of the Lord's Prayer, by which everything said above is confirmed. Malum: "evil," that is, the devil. Bonum: "good," that is, Christ. We approach God not by bodily steps but by the intent of the mind; for we draw near to God or move away from him not in place but in mind. Ducit: "guides." The line and the half-line are Virgil's: one line and a half. Et bona libertas: "and good freedom," because they can escape, can flee. Per pascua: "through the pastures," that is, through the dwellings of the heavenly Jerusalem. The pasture is the sweetness of the divine vision.

Bridal chambers: for “weddings.” In Greek, thalame means pleasure; hence the name thalamus for the place where pleasure is consummated. In the water jars: he calls the water jars “basins” (lacus), and these are named from “lying hidden” (latendo), because the waters lay hidden there. Hydor is Greek for water; hence hydriae is the name for vessels made to hold water. Joys: this is a fancy, a kind of poetic imagining, since he gives feeling to a thing without feeling, so that they ceased to be what they were and began to be what they were not. Unsetting grapes: the unfailing faithful, who will never perish. The vine-shoot (pampinus) is the leaf of the vine, which protects the clusters from the heat of the sun and the harm of the rains. In the same way, divine protection shields and fortifies the faithful of the holy Church against the adversaries of this world, so that they do not fail. After: afterward, once he had turned the water into wine. Fever: fever (febris) is named from “being hot” (fervendo). Although it is named from heat, it is sometimes cold, and in divine Scripture all illnesses go by the name of fever. How much command: that is, power. This is an exclamation of wonder. We say “how much” of some thing, as in “how much wine,” “how much water.” Countryside: farmsteads. Cottages: shepherds' houses. Fort (castellum): a diminutive from castra, “camp.” Wretched in his whiteness: others rejoiced because of their whiteness, but he was saddened, because leprosy rejoices in the body. Lepra in Greek means mottling; hence a leper is someone whose body is blotched with various colours. It is asked why the leper met the Lord on the road. The reason is that the law commanded every leper to be separated from the fellowship of the common dwelling. Fever: although fever is named from heat, it sometimes torments the body with cold. In death: in doubtful death. Funus, “death,” is named from funes, “cords,” that is, candles; candles are cords coated with wax. Was burning: because a fever is cold at first and hot afterward. By “spring” he means the woman's faith, which lay hidden in her heart. Rages: he means the harassments of the black ones. This is not because spirits are black, for colour belongs only to bodies. Rather, we call the damned or the dead “black” (nigros) from the Greek nekros. The evil spirits are called black because of their malice, since, although they live forever, they are dead to eternal happiness. By “honour” he means man, because man is the honour of all natures, for through him all things are honoured. He knew: that is, Christ. In his substance the devil belongs to God, because God created him. But insofar as he is evil, he does not belong to God, because God created him good and made all things very good. Dry seaweed: dry plants. Seaweed (algae) is the name for the refuse of the sea [?] or of anything else. He therefore went to places by the sea so that there he might show [?] that he was true God. Skiffs: little boats. Cymba is Greek, cumba Latin. Were poising: were stretching, were moderating. Librare properly means to raise something up on high. A raft (ratis) is properly a joining-together of beams or a stack of timbers. Blasts: winds; hence flabellum, a diminutive meaning a little wind. Winter is the fourth part of the year, but the word is used loosely for a storm. Squalls: great waves. A squall is wind mixed with water. Salt shallows: the salty [?] waters of the sea. It is poetic that he says “salt,” since the Sea of Galilee has fresh water, fit for drinking. He says this because the sea in general is named from its bitterness. One should also know that the Lord's voyages are said to have been on the Sea of Galilee. Shipwrecks: perilous; they thought they were going to suffer shipwreck. To sleep is to rest; to doze is to grow sluggish and drowsy before rest. Quick: quickly. These are the words of frightened men, for among the frightened speech is not continuous but broken. Leaping out: rejoicing because of Christ. Eager: greedy. Winds are said to have wings because of their speed. Sprang forth: leapt out with a rush. He said “twin” because there were two. Evils: punishments. Legion: a legion is 6,666 demons. In Greek a legion is called keras, and in Macedonian phalanx. Double: because inwardly they were pervaded by demons and outwardly entangled in chains. According to their deserts: because it was fitting for the unclean to seek the clean [?]. Oletum and olidum (“stinking”) are the same, and they are words of middle meaning (ton meson); therefore they always need an epithet, that is, an adjective. Phalanxes: multitudes. It is a word in the language of the Medes for what we call legions. Bristling, grim, horrible: three epithets without a conjunction, a figure called asyndeton. Without use: without function. When he says “loosened,” he shows what paralysis is. Lysis means loosing, paralysis loosening; hence a paralytic is someone loosened throughout his limbs. Bonds: joints. The sinews are the bonds of the body; when they are loosened, they make the body slack and limp. Ills: infirmities. Infirmity is given in five ways. First, for the glory of God, so that God may be praised, as with Lazarus and the man born blind. Second, to guard virtues, as with Paul, so that he would not grow arrogant through such greatness. Third, to increase virtues, as with Tobit and Job, who became holier by bearing infirmity patiently. Fourth, on account of sins, as with this paralytic. The fifth way is that of the reprobate, who begin to be tormented here so that through these torments they may pass on to eternal ones, as happened to Herod and Antiochus. With a welcome reward: a reciprocal one, because he was carrying the bed that had carried him. This is said by periphrasis. Closed: last. Functa for defuncta, “dead.” Grown: matured, because she was twelve years old and already fit for marriage. He says “hope” because in her lay the hope of descendants. Funeral: corpse. Flooding: flowing forth. Her name is the haemorrhoissa, the woman whose blood was flowing. Haima is Greek for blood, and rheo means “I flow back.” He calls the fringe of Christ's garment a “thread.” It was the custom among the Jews to put hyacinth-blue threads on the four corners of the cloak, so that these would distinguish them from other nations. Mourning: “mourning” is used by metonymy. The rooftops of the sorrowful house: the weeping house, in which there were people weeping. The container stands for what it contains. Dying for dead. Anxious: uncertain. Wailing is a word of middle meaning (ton meson): “wailing” is used both of an army in pursuit and of an army in flight. Funereal: suited to a funeral, with the pipes sounding. It is the power of the art of music to make the joyful more joyful and those who grieve grieve more. Lamentation: mourning. Frequent: great. Turned: “songs” is understood. Those who had earlier wept from grief now lament because of unexpected joy. There seems to be a contradiction between what the evangelist says, “the girl is dead,” and what the Lord says, “she is not dead.” Yet both are true: to men she was dead, but to him who could raise her she was not dead but sleeping. Biothanatus: twice dead, for thanatos means “mortal” and athanatos “immortal.” Renowned: noble, for kleos means glory. He is called Son of David, and not of the other fathers, because the promises about the Son of God were made especially to David. Cognosce for cognoscere. Torpid: growing sluggish, failing. But the house of Israel: he commanded them to go only into Israel, so that the Jews would have no occasion to say, “They go to others and abandon us.” By this name: that they should be called Israel. These are the poet's words, set in parenthesis. Freely (gratis) is an adverb from grace (gratia). Grace is a spontaneous gift bestowed on someone without merit. It is as if the Lord were saying: “You are mine, and the sheep are mine, and the pastures are mine. So do not sell the pastures to my sheep, that is, doctrine, or the Holy Spirit, who is given through the laying on of hands.” He said this so that priests would have an example and would not sell the priestly ministry. In paradise there is a certain spring from which four rivers flow. Gihon is the Nile and Pishon is the Ganges; the Tigris and the Euphrates are called by their own names. Synagogue means a gathering together, just as church means a calling together. Measured: diminished. Restored: returning. Takes away nothing: unlike physicians, who usually cut something off the limbs so that the whole body may be healed. Renewing: repairing. Chelydrus: the devil. Cherson means land and hydor water; hence the chelydrus is a serpent, because it can live on land and in water. Looking down: gazing downward. Unbroken: continuous. He says “unbroken” so that you would not suppose the illness ran on for only some of those years. They seek the depths: they gape after earthly wealth. To gape after is to strain toward. Here he allegorizes. That woman signifies those who are weighed down by the burden of sins and delight in earthly wealth. Greater: greater miracles than those Moses performed. It was a greater thing to satisfy a great multitude from two fish and five loaves than from an immense bounty of quail. Coturnix and ortygometra are the same, namely the quail. Cophinus, corbis and canthara are the same. Increased: enlarged. So great an abundance of fragments was gathered as had not been set out. Day: the sun. Pallor: blackness. It is poetic that he says “snatching,” for poets say that the sun sinks into the ocean in the evening and rises in the east in the morning. Hesperus is a star that rises after sunset; at midnight it is called Venus, and in the morning Lucifer. Plains: the flat expanse of the sea. Plains are whatever supports something: the plains of birds are the field [?], the plains of ships the sea, the plains of men the land. Grey-green: of a green colour. Glaucus means green, but it is a colour between white and black. Beneath a footpath: beneath the passage of feet. Gennesaret is a region across the Sea of Galilee. It is called Gennesar, “producing a breeze for itself,” just as the sea produces a storm. How many: how great. Tyre and Sidon are cities by the sea. Tyre is interpreted as “narrowness” and Sidon as “hunting”; Tyre was earlier also called Sarra … [?] For the fault: the infirmity. Ham was the son of Noah after whom all the Canaanites are named. Fragrant (odoratae): because it receives its scent from foods. Odorum is what gives off a scent of itself; odoratum is what receives it from elsewhere, like a garment; odorisecum is what follows a scent, like a dog. Among the brambles: in the error of paganism. From the grass: from the teaching of the gospel, from the knowledge of the divine Scriptures, which were given to the Hebrews. At that time the Hebrews believed in God, while the other nations did not yet believe; hence the Psalmist says: “God is known in Judah.” Tunes: fits together. He calls the functions of the limbs an “instrument,” for our body consists, as it were, of the working of the art of music. Just as the art of music is tuned outwardly by strings, so the body is tuned by the balance of the elements. Bodily sickness is nothing other than an imbalance of the elements, and health is their balance. Instruments: the harmony of the limbs. The sinews are the bonds of the body. To be doubled: to be multiplied. If they went home fasting, the very toil of the journey would increase their hunger. Which: the crowd. Enormous: immeasurable. Norma means a rule or measure; hence enormis is used of something so large that its measure cannot be found. Of the second: female. The first sex is male, the second female. And of the second age: children. Or [?] the first age is infancy, the second childhood. Its remnants and heaps are the same thing. This is epexegesis, which occurs when one thing is said twice in different words. Of the baskets: a sporta is a vessel woven from palm leaves. He said poetically that hunger itself was terrified, and he calls the leftovers themselves a harvest. Lamp: lychnus in Greek, lucerna in Latin. Bright: this is the common figure, which in Greek is called koinou. Unknown: because they had not seen them before. Alpha is the first letter of the Greeks and omega the last. Enachos [?], although it comes after them, is not a letter but a numeral sign. These letters signify “God, the beginning and the end,” as he himself says in the Apocalypse: “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last.” Christ is understood as the beginning through Moses, who lived in the third age of the world, and as the end through Elijah, who lived in the fifth age, close to the sixth, and is still alive. Or else he stood between Elijah and Moses because he himself is the beginning and the end of prophecy. On the threshold of life: standing at the entrance, as it were at the door of the resurrection, because the last age had now come, in which the elect were to rise again and pass over to eternal life. Cast down in his eyes: a figurative expression meaning having his eyes cast down. The lowering of his eyes shows his humility. Tribute: tax (vectigal), which is named from “carrying” (vehendo). The whole world paid a census tax to Caesar: in the fifth year one gold coin, over the next five years one silver coin, and over the next five a bronze one. Three times five is fifteen, and this is the indictum or indiction. Bearer: carrier, namely the fish that had in its mouth a stater, that is, two drachmas. A drachma is a kind of coin that weighs ten denarii; hence it is called this as though it were a tenth part of a drachma [?]. In another sense, a drachma is two and a half denarii. A stater is the same thing; moreover, the thing on which something is weighed is called a statera, a balance. In yet another sense, dragma is Greek for what is fabula, a story, in Latin; hence a dramatic poem is called a fabulous one. Of the hall: in the hall, in the palace. Aula is named from aulaea, curtains. An aula is a royal house. Not in years, because we cannot be, as the Apostle says: “Be children in malice, but in understanding be mature.” Nor leaning back: proud. We call the proud “leaning back,” because they usually walk leaning back and holding themselves upright.

Placid: calm. Judea in a general sense means the whole kingdom of the Jews, but in a specific sense that southern part in which lay Jerusalem and the tribe of Judah and of Benjamin, together with the priestly tribe; this too is called Judea. Camel (camelus) comes from the Greek camir, "curved"; for it is a curved animal, curved and humped, suited to carrying burdens. Fertility: abundance. To will: his will is his deed. To grow mild: to grow cheap. Sense: substance, by taking [?] from them their anxiety about riches. This is impossible: that a rich man who loves riches should enter the kingdom of heaven. But to God on high all things [?] are possible, because he can bring it about that a rich man gives his riches to the poor and, having become poor, follows God. Verdigris (aerugo) and rust (rubigo) are a corruption of metals; but aerugo, the blight of crops, is named from gold (aurum), because it has a golden colour. The moth is a worm that consumes whatever it wears away, and it belongs to clothing, whereas verdigris belongs to gold. Nor does it serve: obey; for here gold serves thieves when it lets itself be carried off. To settle (considere), from the verb sido, sidis; considere means to sit down, to remain. Wandering breezes: the empty air. Bethany is a little village on the side of the Mount of Olives, a thousand paces from Jerusalem. The fig (ficus) is named from fruitfulness (fecunditas), for sometimes it has ripe fruit, sometimes unripe. He said "leafen" (frondea) for "leafy" (frondosa). Frondeus means what is made of leaves, of twigs, from which a booth or shelter is made; frondosus means what has leaves, like a tree. Hungry, he found: the Lord did not look for fruit on the fig tree for that reason, nor because he did not know that it was not the season; and according to the evangelist it was not the season for it to have fruit. What sin, then, had the tree committed? None; but that tree signifies the synagogue of the Jews, where the Lord found no fruit, and therefore he cursed it. Trunk: stipes is properly the trunk from which the branches grow; here he has used it for the whole tree. Of sap: of greenness. To widow (uiduare) is to forsake; hence a widow is a woman forsaken. Nurtures nothing fertile: nothing good. Now he allegorizes. Allegory is inversion, when one passes from the letter to the spiritual sense. Pleasant: beautiful. A place is called pleasant (amoenus) when it is suited to delight. Palm: the palm (palma) is so called as though from pacis alma, "nurturer of peace," because it is given to victors, or because it is shaped like a hand. And the righteous man is fittingly compared to the palm, because the palm does not have its strength and foundation in its root, as other trees do, but is slender, and thick at the top, and has its foundation there; so too the saints do not look to the earth or care for earthly things, but have all their strength in heavenly things. Lebanon is a mountain in Judea where cedars grow, very tall trees; and Lebanon means "whitening." By keeping silent: because by keeping silent he showed that he was mute, whereas people usually make their infirmities known by speaking. Pharisees means "the separated," who on account of their special holiness separated themselves from the rest of the people. They are named from Perez (Phares), son of Judah. Leaning over: standing behind. With fragrant nard: precious, sweet-smelling. Cherishing: anointing. The Lord's feet signify his lowly members; he washes the Lord's feet with tears and wipes them with his hair who has compassion on the poor and counts their need as his own. He cherishes them with ointment when he gives off the fragrance of a good name. For no hand is empty of a gift when the threshing floor of the heart is full of good will. Capernaum is a city situated on Mount Tabor. Synagogue means "congregation," just as church means "calling together" or "assembly." Among the Jews there was a house called the synagogue, into which they gathered on the sabbath day to hear and teach the law, as is now done in church. Insolent: horrible; proteruus is so called as though porro toruus, "exceedingly grim," very horrible. What have we and you: what is there in common, or what concerns us. Why have you come to destroy us: to condemn. And holy—: [we know] you to be the Son of God [?]. For they spoke of lesser things to the demons [?], to whom it was granted in some way to know the holy Son of God; but the lesser things [?] they did not know, until his glory and might broke open hell. For although the demons lost their dignity, they did not lose their nature. For, as Augustine says, they are animals with bodies of air, eternal in spirit, malignant in mind; and they are of a subtler nature, and therefore they sometimes foresee future things. Three things were hidden from the devil: the virgin's giving birth, the divinity of the man, the passion of the Redeemer. Demonas has a Greek accent, and therefore it is shortened. Forbids: he does not wish to be proclaimed by such a witness, because [praise] is not precious in the mouth of a sinner. Of black death: he says "black death" from the Greek nicros. For we call the dead "black," just as we call the living "white." Friend: we say amicum illius ("his friend"); amicum illi [?]; [the one] is possessive, amicus illi ("a friend to him") is acquisitive. Skimming (legens): sailing; hence Virgil: "they skim with sails," that is, they sail. Breathing-passages: he calls the senses so, through which we breathe. The inner chambers burst open: the inner parts unlocked. A penetrale is a hidden place that is penetrable, that is, can be entered. Lying prostrate: condemned in the eyes [?]. He calls blindness the appearance of feigned death, because the dead do not see. Pools: the sea. A pool (stagnum) is so called from standing (stare), where water stands still. In the alder: in a boat. The alder is a species of tree from which ships are made; he puts the species for the genus. Watery nations: fishes. He calls fishes nations, as Virgil does bees: "they lead out the grown young of the nation"; and the same poet of fishes, when speaking of Proteus: "around him went the wet nation of the vast sea." Funeral rites: exequiae are the services rendered to the dead, named from carrying out (exequi). Funeral (funus): death; funus means death, from funes, that is, candles. Candles are cords coated with wax. Urn: the burial either of a husband or of a son. Among the ancients an urn was a vessel in which the ashes of the dead were customarily laid away; hence it is used for burial; it is also the same as a memorial. Bier: feretrum is Greek; in Latin it is capulus, from capere, "to take." Feretrum and faretra ("quiver") come from one Greek word, foron, "to carry." For the one carries the dead, the other death. Sitting up and speaking are two signs of life; and it is a hysterologia, for first he came back to life, then he sat up. White procession: that is, joyful glory. It was an ancient custom to wear dark, black garments in adversity and grief, but white in prosperity and joy; this is what he means by "white procession." Squameus for squamosus ("scaly"). The serpent is called scaly because it has scales, like a fish, after the manner of a coat of mail, which makes them invulnerable. Gehenna is compounded of ge and enna and means "free valley"; for ge means "valley" in Hebrew, and Hennon was a man from whom that valley was named. The children of Israel fled to it, departing from the temple of God because of the pleasantness of the place, and there they worshipped idols, because the spring of Siloam watered it. Then they perished there in two ways: in soul, because they worshipped idols, and in body, because they were slain by their enemies. Hence Gehenna is used for hell, because there is a twofold punishment there: heat and cold. Seven coils: seven revolutions; the same as sevenfold windings. The number seven stands for fullness, because the whole time of this world revolves through seven days; hence he used seven for the fullness of the demons that were in her. Viperous: the poisons of the devil. The viper (vipera) is so called because it gives birth by force (ui pariat), for the young come out by killing their mother. Ceasing: resting. You feigned: you pretended. Living wickedly, you wanted to show yourselves good by miracles, and while you were doing wicked things you pretended to be doing divine works. There are some who, when they see people working miracles, pay attention not to their life but to the miracles; but God looks to a good life rather than to miracles. By spells: by incantations. Shapes: not true but false. The story is well known: the rod was turned into a real serpent. For God has power to change his creature into whatever he wishes. Magicians, however, have no power over creation, but bewitch, that is, deceive, the eyes of those who watch. Fascinum means envious praise; hence fascino, fascinas ("to bewitch"). After: hereafter. Easy: gentle; for it is the custom of the rich to be invited only with difficulty, but the Lord had come to the Pharisee's house at an easy request. Perez (Phares) was the son of Judah, from whom the Pharisees are named; and the name means "the separated." Into the expanse of the belly: as though he had become all belly. Dropsy (hydrops): hydor is Greek for water, hence hydropicus, "watery." Dropsy is a disease beneath the skin, and in Latin it is called ueternus; the dropsical disease arises from a defect of the bladder, with a swollen belly and foul breath. Flowing: because the more he drinks, the more he thirsts. Lake: the dropsical man's body; he calls the belly a lake, the water being in it as in a lake. The Lord used to visit the houses of leading men, not because he needed their banquets, but for the sake of their servants, who, held back by their service, could not come to him and hear his preaching; for he cared for all alike. Portents: a portent is something that appears suddenly and foreshows something. A prodigy is the same [?]: a sign that only appears suddenly and signifies nothing. Leprosy: leprosy is scurf or itch or eruption, because putrid humour flows from the body; leprosy itself is a portent. Obscene: with the foul. We call birds obscene that bring an evil omen, an augury, and then the word is compounded from the verb cano ("to sing"); but obscenus meaning "foul" is compounded from caenum, that is, from mud. Returned: turned back. Redux is said of one who comes back from some danger. For Christ is the true priest, who offered himself and no other victim on the altar of the cross for the salvation of the world.
