Melchizedek means "king of righteousness": melch "king," sedech "of righteousness"; he showed forth Christ by name and by deed. By deed, because Christ instituted bread and wine as the mystery of his body and blood, just as Melchizedek is read to have been the first to offer bread and wine to God in sacrifice. Importunate: troublesome, persistent. A port is the station and resting place of ships; hence importunus is so called as being "without port" and without rest. Of one mind: dear, faithful. He sought bread: he asked for it. One says peto te illam rem and peto a te illam rem ("I ask you for that thing"). The doors being shut: fores are properly doors that open outward, ualuae those that open inward. Insistently and confidently: he uses so many adverbs to show the persistence of the one refusing. Sojourner: foreigner. An accola is one who comes from elsewhere and dwells in a foreign land. Vault: the testudo is so called because it is made in the likeness of this animal, the tortoise. A testudo is the curved vault of a house, which was made in temples after the likeness of a booth. Testudo is also the close formation of shields by which soldiers' heads were protected, after the likeness of the tortoise, which is protected by a very hard shell. To passable ways: to the uprightness of good works. A place is pervious (peruius) where there is a way. Guilt: every fault that makes one guilty. Of the adulteress: moechus means adulterer; hence the mechanical art gets its name, which is practised with such subtlety that it deceives the eyes of the onlooker. Through the barriers: through the orbs of the eyes. Of kindred clay: he deliberately said "kindred," because man and clay are akin and close to each other. For man, formed from clay, returns to clay. Mystic: the Greeks call a secret mysticen; hence Christ's miracles are called mystical, because, though they were performed bodily, they nevertheless point to something spiritual. Born [blind]: because we were in darkness. This blind man signifies the human race. By the spittle the wisdom of God is signified. For breath flows down from the head into the mouth; in the same way wisdom flows down, as she herself says through Solomon: "I came forth from the mouth of the Most High." So the Lord made clay from spittle and earth, because divinity was joined to human nature. He allegorizes. By the spittle is understood divinity, by the earth humanity, which, joined together in Christ, became the cause of our salvation. Washed: he shortened the vowel for the sake of the metre. Bethany is a little town at the foot of the Mount of Olives, not far from Jerusalem, fifteen stadia away, and it means "house of obedience." Lazarus means "helped." Populatio: that is, a multitude of people; it is an affected, newly coined word. God wept as man, because impassible divinity is not subject to suffering. After the funeral: after death. Funus is properly the corpse of a dead person, named from funes, that is, candles. Deadly chaos: mortal confusion. The law perishes: the law of death is that it keeps what it has once received and never gives it back. Fleeting heights: transitory honours. Trappings: [?]. Phalerae is the general term for all the ornaments of horses; in Greek they are called ephippia. Purple (ostrum): purple dye. Ostrum is so called from oysters (ostrea), small shellfish with whose blood it is dyed. Gold: a golden bridle. It is a sign of a fine horse that it casts bloody foam from its mouth. Honos for honor ("honour"). Was not unequal: this ass was of equal dignity with the one that recognized Christ in the manger. On solid ground: on hard ground. He addresses the Gentiles.

"Had begun": the day had arrived on which the Jews were to celebrate the Passover. Pascha is named from "passing over," not from "passion" (passio), as some say, for on that day the children of Israel passed out of Egypt. Among the Jews the Pasch was the lamb that was sacrificed in the evening. "Glory": the majesty of Christ. It is a fine figure of speech when a quality is named by circumlocution in place of the person, as Virgil calls Hector "the strength of the Trojans"; in the same way Christ is called "the glory of the Lord." "That I may glorify": in the resurrection. "In harmony": in fellowship; because he had called on the Father, the Father answered him. The voice was not God the Father in substance. The dove was not the Holy Spirit, and it was not begotten from other doves but formed from the air. In the same way this voice was not the Father in substance but a sign, to show that Christ was the Son of God. "Yearly": what was celebrated every year; "yearly" means universal, because every year, in the first month, April, called Nisan in Hebrew, the Passover is celebrated among the Jews. Note that the Jews had no system of reckoning but counted the month and the moon by thirty days. On the first day of the month they reckoned the first day of the moon, on the tenth day the tenth, on the fourteenth day the fourteenth, and then the lamb was sacrificed and the Passover was held. "According to custom": in eating the lamb with his disciples, following the custom of the Jews. "Lowly": humilis is so called as if meaning "bending down." A sepulchre is white in appearance outside but inside is full of the corruption of the dead; it is called sepulchrum as if "without pulse" (sine pulsu), without breath. Livor properly means the swelling of bruises, but it is sometimes used for envy, as in this passage. "Having bargained": promising, pledging. Paciscor has two perfects, pepigi and pactus sum, and it is a polysemous word with many meanings. Paciscor means "I make peace" and "I promise," as here. Paciscor also means "I obtain," as when Virgil says "to bargain death for glory," that is, to obtain it. Nomisma (coin) is named from nomen (name), because a denarius is stamped with the king's name. "From a barren mother": would that his mother had been barren, so that he could not have been born. "A better lot": fortune. The poet's first wish is that he had not been born, and if born, that he had died quickly. "Poured forth": born. "Standard-bearer": carrying the signal, for he gave the signal with a kiss. "You press" means "you press upon." "Peace into swords": into battles. He used "swords" for war: the effect is understood through what produces it. "Or": a wolf never kisses a lamb. "Servant": Malchus. "Refrain": stop. Parco has many meanings, "I indulge" or "I preserve"; that is why we call bees "thrifty" (parcas), as preservers of honey. Parco also means "I cease," as here. "Winged": bearing wings. A concilium is the assembled crowd itself, a consilium is the matter being discussed, and a conciliabulum is the place itself. "A thousand": a finite number put for an infinite one. "With empty embers": with opinions, or with evil intent. Favilla (ember) is the food of fire and is named from the Greek phagein, "to eat." "To strike": to beat. In Greek, kolaptein means to strike, which gives colaphus, a blow on the neck; or "to beat" means to give slaps. "Applauded": favoured, smiled on, because before this we were under the devil's slavery. An alapa is a blow to the face, named from the broad palm (lata palma). "Undone": unfinished, yet done. "Decree": promise. "He condemned": he punished. The deed he did when he was forgetful, he condemned when he remembered. "Yield": withdraw. "Offences": an offence (delictum) is when we leave undone what we ought to do, and it is so called as if derelictum, "abandoned." Rigeo makes the perfect rigui; from it comes derigeo, "I make hard." "Trade": prices. Commercium is the exchange of goods (merces). "And he threw it into the corbanan": the corbanan is the treasury where the people's gifts were stored. Corban means "gift," and from it comes corbanan, the place of gifts, where kings and princes deposited gifts on the sabbath. "In vain": casses means spiders' webs, and from it comes the adverb incassum, "uselessly." "May overturn": may subvert. "Sounder": more just. "Choking": constricting, suffocating. He was rightly hanged by the throat, because with it he spoke evil of Christ. Judas perished between heaven and earth, and some say on a fig tree, because he was not worthy to be received by these elements. "Runaway": one going backward. Apostata is Greek; in Latin it means one turned back, or one going back. From it come the verb apostato, apostatas, and the noun apostasia, the thing itself, a going back. This Judas was an apostate, because he left the fellowship of the apostles and joined himself to the blindness of the Jews. "To the throat": to beheading. The iugulum is close to the neck, which is why we use iugulare for "to behead." "Grove": a lucus is a pleasant, wooded place. The Jews worshipped idols in woods and on high places. An idol is so called as if from eidos doulos, "the servitude of a form," and idolum derives from idea as formula derives from forma. "Then": in ancient times. Barabbas means "son of their father, the devil": bar is Greek for "son" and abba means "father." Spelled Barrabas, with two r's, it means "son of their master," for rabbi in Hebrew is magister (master) in Latin. "He was ordered": Christ suffered for all, even for the robber. "All" is not always meant universally but sometimes particularly, for the Lord did not suffer for the wicked. "Grim sickle": a sickle is the iron used to cut hay. The sickle signifies the curse of the Jews, when they said: "His blood be upon us and upon our children." As hay is cut by a sickle, so the Jews were cut down by that curse. "Watchful": shrewd. Lavisse ("to have washed") is used for lavare ("to wash"). "Sacred": what grants pardon. "A reed fills his hand": by saying "fills" he shows that it was large. Arundo is the same as ferula (a fennel stalk). "A feeble sceptre": weak, because it is a slender, pliant plant. "Empty": because it has no pith. "And soon": after he had been mocked; Christ was mocked in another's clothes. He allegorizes: when Christ received this borrowed garment he laid aside his own, and then took his own back again. This signifies that he would lay aside mortal flesh and, in rising, take it up again immortal. "As changeable": mortal. "Wine with gall": myrrh and gall make wine extremely bitter. "Of peril": of punishment. Supplicium means torment. He chose the cross so that we might more easily save ourselves from the devil and his deceits by making the sign of the cross. If he had been stoned, as the Jews wished, we would carry a stone as his sign. By his cross the Lord holds the whole world together, as he himself says: "When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself." So when the Lord was placed on the cross, he held the east with his head, the west with his feet, the north with his right hand and the south with his left. These are the four parts of the world, which in Greek are called: east anatole, west dysis, north arktos, south mesembria. "Gathers": joins. This title was written in three languages. It was written in Hebrew because of divine Scripture, so that, as the apostle says, every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father; so the Jews, whether they like it or not, confess that Christ is king of the Jews. It was written in Greek because of human wisdom, for the Greeks invented many arts, and in Latin because of Roman power, for the Romans ruled over almost all nations. "With the spoils": with plunder. Exuviae are properly the hides of wild beasts stripped from their limbs, but by extension the word is used for any spoil. Schisma is Greek for a tearing; from it come the schismatics, heretics who tear themselves away from the catholic faith. Though Christ and the robbers received the same sentence, the punishment of the cross, they did not deserve it equally, for Christ hung there for our salvation. "Sentence": judgement. "Beas" [?] is a neutral word (to meson), used in both a good and a bad sense. It has a bad sense in this line, where these men are guilty and condemnable to the world. It has a good sense in the following line, where the world is "guilty," that is, bound and in debt, because it owes him eternal fidelity. Insults (convicia) are named from neighbours (vicini), because neighbours hurl abuse at one another. "Gathers": unites. He makes an apostrophe to paradise. It is Eden in Hebrew, paradisus in Greek, hortus (garden) in Latin. "Violent": put for great violence. Facinus (deed) is a neutral word, like facio, from which it is derived, for sometimes people speak of a good facinus. "The sky": the heavens. He named not a part of it but the whole, because a natural eclipse covers only part of the sky; but this one was not natural, it was a sign. Note too that an eclipse of the sun never happens except on the thirtieth or the first day of the moon, and at that time it was the fourteenth. "With funeral rites": with services. Exequiae are so called because they follow (sequuntur) the bodies of the dead. "Lay hidden": hid itself. Delitesco is compounded from lateo. "Not to last long": that is, the sun's light itself, except for three hours. "Mystical": figurative. The space of three hours signified that the Lord would lie three days in the tomb. From the sixth hour to the ninth is the three hours during which the sun was hidden. He translated word for word when he said "mystical," meaning "secret," for the Greeks call a secret thing mystikon. "Nor was the earth without disaster": without harm. He has already spoken of the heavens, and now he tells how the earth grieved along with them. "Last": final. Suppremus with a double p means "last" and comes from the verb supprimo, but it could not be used here because of the metre; supremus with a single p signifies the most high God. "The summit": the loftiness of Christ. "To sink down": to fall down, thinking to go down to hell with its maker. "Wandering": changeable. "The lost": the human race. "Things that stand": things that abide, the world. "With a little brush": the sponge, which they put around hyssop with a reed. "To bastards": to those born of a harlot. He calls the Jews born of a harlot because they deserted Christ, the husband of their soul, and followed Barabbas the robber, choosing him as an adulterer. Vinegar is made from the best wine, and acetum is so called as if "acid," sour. So too the Jews were born of fathers, of the patriarchs. "Hateful offspring": a hostile generation. "Good": Christ is called bonus from the Greek boō, "I call," because he calls all by his natural goodness. "He gave up": because he died of his own will. Death did not come upon him as it comes upon men. "God not perishing": the divinity not dying. Obeo means "I go around" and also "I die." "They gape": they are loosened abundantly. Hio, hias means "I open my mouth." It forms the inchoative hisco, hiscis, from which fatisco is compounded with the Greek fatos [?], "much." From this come the adverb affatim and the verb fatisco, which means "abundantly." "With a crash": with a sound. Fragor means a great noise, derived from things broken (fracta). He calls the body of Christ the greater temple, because it was full of divinity. "Of its nursling": of its companion. As one comrade mourns another, or a disciple his master, so the temple mourned Christ. He says poetically that, seeing Christ die, the temple laid bare its breast in grief. This follows the custom of the Jews, who tore their clothing when some grief befell them. Note that there were two veils in the temple, an inner one and an outer one, and it was the outer one that was torn. "Is laid open": is opened. He shows what the tearing of the veil signifies, namely the unsealing of the law. As the face of Moses was covered with a veil, so before Christ's coming the law was covered by a carnal and literal understanding. "Did not form": did not create you. "Viper's": serpent's. He says poetically that death had as its father the serpent by which the first man was led astray, and as its mother the sin which that same man committed. "For a time": he says "for a time" because Christ was soon to rise again, after the third day. "By ecbasis": by digression; said when he returns to the narrative. "And open": laid open. Cruor is named from running (currendo); as long as it runs, blood is also called cruor. "By its occupant": by its inhabitant. "Noble": that is, the place, because of him who lay there. "More noble": because of him who rose from there. "Increased": was multiplied. "And should report": that those disciples should say. "Sealed": with the governor's ring. They sealed the tomb with a seal and a stamp from the ring of Pilate himself. "With watches": with vigils. Excubiae means daytime watches, just as vigiliae means night watches. "Sabbath": sabbata and the singular sabbatum both denote a single day. By speaking of the seventh day, he recalls the last day and shows that the Lord's day, which follows, is the first, because all the time of this world revolves in seven days. "With a gift": with ointment made of spices. Spice is a kind of ointment, and it is gathered like a harvest. "Dispensing": or completing what was needed for the Lord's burial. "With angelic faith": by the faithful report of the angel. The angel appeared in the form of fire to terrify the guards. "Sleeping": asleep. Exuviae are the garments of the dead. "To loose": to untie. "Covered": clothed, covered over. "To carry off": to carry. A thief never likes delay. "About to perish": the figure apo koinou, "from the common [element]." "No trumpet": the festival at which you sound the trumpet. "No anointed one": your king. "Nor your victim": because on the calends and the new moons the Jews offered victims, gave alms and held great feasts. "Darkened": blackened. The synagogue was at first the bride of Christ, but afterwards, by worshipping idols, it became an adulteress. In its place Christ took the Church to himself, as the apostle says: "He betrothed to himself a Church without spot or wrinkle." The Blessed Virgin Mary prefigures the Church, for she was chaste and a virgin before and after giving birth. In the same way the Church daily bears children to God spiritually in baptism and yet remains chaste in the integrity of her faith. "Spreading abroad": announcing; this is poetic. "Informant": she who made known that Christ had returned. He appeared to two disciples going to the village of Emmaus and made himself known in the breaking of bread. "Broiled": roasted. "Like apostates": unbelievingly. "Thomas": the name means "abyss." "Didymus" means "doubtful" or "most like," because he was partly like Christ. "Threshold": door. "Whoever": a magician. The magic art always wants to stay hidden and never to show itself, and a magician does not like those who inquire into his art. "Hanging": suspended. "Wave-wandering": fish, which wander in the waves. "The way": the reason; it is not without mystery. "The net was full": 154 [?]. This number signifies the number of the elect. He calls preaching a net, because as fish are gathered by a net, so the souls of the godly are gathered by the preaching of the disciples. "To the worthy": to the faithful. "Is enclosed": is caught. As they cast the net on the right side, so Christ places his own on the right-hand side of blessedness. "In their arms": in their arms. "To the footsteps": to imitation. Olene is Greek for "elbow," which is why part of the arm is called ulna. "One": that is, faith. "To stand firm": to remain. He allegorizes: the fish, the water: baptism. Christ is the bread, as he himself says: "I am the living bread." The Holy Spirit is the fire, because the Holy Spirit appeared to the disciples in tongues of fire on the day of Pentecost. From this comes the water of baptism. "For a banquet": for eating a meal. "With modest provision": with small preparation, small and not luxurious, unlike what kings and princes usually prepare. "By rite": by custom, because the ancients reclined on couches when they dined. "On couches": on the grass, where they reclined with their master. "To the labourer": to Peter; by "sheep" he means preachers. Bethany is a small town on the Mount of Olives, and its name means "obedient house." The right hand signifies equal glory. The Lord does not have a right hand; "right hand" is used to mean equality and power. "Very many" of his countless good works: the disciples did not write down everything the Lord did, but only as much as bears on the salvation of the human race; if they had written everything, the world could not have contained it. Carta (paper) is named from the town of Cartanum, where the use of paper was first discovered, just as parchment (pergamentum) is named from the town of Pergamum. Cartae are membranes, and membranes are the skins of sheep, so called because they are stripped from the sheep's limbs (membra). Having described the miracles, the poet urges everyone to sing with him to Christ and give thanks.

"Honour": glory. "With our mouth." "Holy": that is, glorious. Paractera is Greek for "echoing back." From it comes the paracteric poem, so called because one verse is echoed by another: the beginning of the first becomes the end of the second. "Of one": of Adam. "For the merit": for the cause. "The lesser": that is, descendants. "Of one": of Christ. "Who lay open": she was the door, because death entered through her. He calls Judas the wicked brother, because Christ calls all his disciples brothers. "Passing": the translation of Enoch. "What he lost": what kind of place he lost. "Let them make ready": let them prepare. This concerns Christ's passing, because we too shall pass over in the same way. "The waters": the flood. Noah's ark was made of smoothed, hewn timber and was not very heavy. In the same way the righteous do not carry the weight of crimes. "The supreme victim" is Isaac. "Silent": hidden, because it concealed Christ's future sacrifice. "Unlocks": opens. "Heir": Jacob, to whom Isaac's inheritance passed. He is speaking of Jacob and how he wrestled with the angel. Jacob was lame because the angel touched him on the sinew; this was for the sake of a mystery, and it is why the Jews do not eat sinews. "The nation": of the Jews. "Limps": in believing. "Venitus" [?]: sold. Venundatus comes from veneo, venis, as if venum eo ("I go for sale"), but venum is not in use. "Brother": of his own brothers. He is speaking of Joseph. "Sold": by Judah. "Drove back": from us. "All things": the whole land of Egypt. He is speaking of Pharaoh. "While they cease": you likewise always perish. "With blood": his own. He is speaking of the lamb which the children of Israel sacrificed at the Passover. With its blood they made marks on their doors, because that night the angel passed through all Egypt killing all the firstborn of Egypt, and where there was blood he did no harm. "Overwhelms": drowns. "Wave": of baptism. "Refreshed": filled. He is speaking of the children of Israel, when God rained manna on them. "Adopts": chooses. He is speaking of the children of Israel, when they worshipped idols. "For itself": by itself. "Proof": a sign. Before the law, people did not know that they had sin; they did not know concupiscence or perceive it to be sin until the law made it known, saying, "You shall not covet your neighbour's property." "Behold the rock": he is speaking of the rock from which the waters flowed. This rock signifies Christ, as the apostle says: "And the rock was Christ." "Gift": burnt offerings. "Seditious": Dathan and Abiram. He is speaking of the children of Israel when they rose up against Moses and wanted to stone him. Then fire came down from heaven on the burnt offering and consumed it, together with most of the camp. Had Aaron not stood between the dead and the living with the censer of incense, nearly everyone would have died. "Heir": the people who came out of Egypt and died in the desert, except Joshua and Caleb. Joshua divided the land among his people; so Christ assigns the blessed kingdoms of the Father to his faithful. "Walls": he speaks of Jericho. When the children of Israel were coming from Egypt, the priests carried the ark around the city for six days, and on the seventh they took it. The ark of God signifies Christ's flesh, or the Church. "Under the fleece": he is speaking of Gideon. When Gideon wanted to fight the Midianites, he asked for a sign: that there should be dew on the fleece while the ground was dry, and the next night dew on the ground while the fleece was dry. "You conquer, O Jephthah." "Nations": the Midianites. He is speaking of Jephthah. When Jephthah was setting out for war, he promised to give God as an offering whatever he met first. He met his own daughter and said: "I will not close my mouth against you, but I will fulfil to God what I have said." Yet he gave her a space of two months to mourn her virginity. Why? Because the law cursed all women who had no offspring. "Affection": love, because he loved God more than his daughter. "Took": took away from us. "Of the commandment": of the Gospel, concerning the new law, where we read: "If anyone strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other." "Defiling": staining. "They move": the hard-hearted Jews to belief. Although they all should have believed and the signs should have moved them, all the hard-hearted Jews refused to believe. "Brought": carried. "To slaves": to the human race. Though he ought to have brought punishments, he brought gifts instead of punishments. "Bore": endured. "Life": Christ. "Tartarus": hell. The depth of hell is called Tartarus, from tartarizein, from trembling, because the depth of anything makes one tremble. "Profane": Adam, sacrilegious, as it were, in sinning. "Hard": rebellious, because his disciples came from among them. "Tasted": drunk, because his blood was shed for our race and we drink of it daily. "Had bound fast": had tightly bound. "Bonds": of love, for the apostles and martyrs, whom they could not frighten with punishment. "Enemies": the hostile Jews. "To hasten": the coming. "Of the signs": of the former prophets. "Our gifts": the body and blood of our [?]. "Of the former": of the prophets. "To the godly": to the holy. "Sects": the Church is full of heresies. "Ravens": the wicked. "The dove": the Church. "Crooked": called twisted, not straight. The vision of Christ will be a reward for the elect and condemnation for the reprobate. Spiritus has a long "spi," but the poet preferred to break the rule rather than diminish the Trinity.

"Carries": bears. "Secrets": heavenly things. "Crushed pledges": the slain children. "Bent": on bended knee. A centurion is so called because he commands a hundred men; in Greek he is a hekatontarchos, just as a chiliarchos commands a thousand men. Chilioi means "a thousand." "With the tears of one pleading": of one making supplication. "Certain women." "Cheromyrrh": dry ointments, as if prepared by hand. Xeros is Greek for "dry" and myron for "ointment"; hence xerophagi are those who eat dry food. From this a shop where ointments are sold is called a myropolium. Pharmacopolium means the same thing: pharmakon is an ointment, and those who sell and prepare it are called myrocopi. Cheir is Greek for "hand" and kopos for "labour," hence chirocopi; from this also comes copia (abundance), because all wealth comes from labour. In the same way, a bibliopolium is a place where books are sold, and their sellers are called Sosii. Sanna is a rude noise made with the nostrils, and so it is also used for mockery. "Sold": by Judas. "Of the most wicked lion": God is called a lion because of his strength, and the devil is called a lion because of his savagery.
